title: The leaky integrate-and-fire neuron, from circuit to spikes
objective: Connect the membrane-as-circuit picture to the integrate-and-fire equation, and see why a constant input either settles below threshold or produces regular spikes.

scenes.title: A membrane as a circuit
scenes.caption: The membrane stores charge like a capacitor and leaks it through open channels towards the leak reversal potential. Multiplying the current balance by R gives the model's equation.

scenes.title: Below threshold: relaxation
scenes.caption: With RI = 15 mV the potential relaxes towards E_L + RI = −55 mV, which is below the threshold of −50 mV, so the model never spikes.
scenes.plotDescription: The membrane potential rises from −70 mV and levels off near −55 mV without reaching the −50 mV threshold.

scenes.title: Above threshold: regular spikes
scenes.caption: With RI = 25 mV the target −45 mV lies above threshold. The potential climbs, is reset to −65 mV at each crossing, and climbs again: a regular spike train. The spike itself is a bookkeeping event, not modelled.
scenes.plotDescription: A sawtooth: the potential repeatedly rises from −65 mV to −50 mV and drops back, several times within 200 ms.

scenes.title: What the model leaves out
scenes.caption: Real spikes come from voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels. The model keeps the passive membrane and replaces the spike with a threshold rule, so it says when a neuron fires, not how.
